scenes.heading: Agent Design Patterns Catalog
scenes.narration: Let's walk the catalog of agent design patterns — the handful of building blocks behind almost every 'agentic' system.

scenes.heading: The five composable patterns
items: Routing: classify, then dispatch to a specialist
Orchestrator-workers: a lead delegates dynamic subtasks
scenes.narration: Most agents are really one of five composable patterns. Prompt chaining runs fixed steps in order. Routing classifies an input, then dispatches it to a specialist handler. Parallelization fans work out and aggregates the results. Orchestrator-workers has a lead LLM decide subtasks at runtime. And evaluator-optimizer loops generate-critique-refine. Each trades control for autonomy differently.

scenes.heading: A dial from controlled to autonomous
steps: One good call enough? Ship it
Steps known in advance? Prompt chaining
scenes.narration: Think of the patterns as a dial from assembly line to general contractor. Walk the questions top to bottom and stop at the first yes. If a single well-prompted call works, just ship it. Only when a concrete limitation forces it do you descend into more structure — because every added step costs latency, dollars, and debugging surface.

scenes.heading: Routing in practice
scenes.narration: Here's the routing pattern concretely. One LLM call classifies a support ticket, then we dispatch to a handler tuned for that category. Each downstream path stays focused instead of cramming every case into one bloated prompt — and easy cases can even go to a cheaper model.

scenes.text: Start with the simplest thing that works. Add orchestration structure only when a concrete limitation forces it — complexity is never a default.
scenes.narration: The single most expensive mistake in the field is reaching for a complex multi-agent framework when one prompt would do. Match the minimum viable structure to the task, and add complexity only when a real limitation forces your hand.
